title: Build a reply in the right order
description:
Implement a handler called GreetHandler. It receives the writer the server hands a handler for building the reply, together with a pointer to the incoming request, and returns nothing.

How the request arrives: the client sends a plain GET, and carries the name in the query string of the url it asks for — GET /greet?name=Ada. Nothing arrives in a request body and nothing arrives in a header, so the name has to be pulled back out of the request's url, where it sits under the key name. A url that gives the key nothing to hold, GET /greet?name=, counts as no name at all, and so does a url that leaves the key out altogether, GET /greet.

How the reply is taken: the handler returns nothing, so the reply is not a value you hand back — you assemble it on the writer you were given. Once the handler ends, that reply is read back the way a client would see it: the status it carries, the headers that actually went out with it, and the body. Each of the three parts described below is checked against what was read back that way.

When a name is supplied, the reply carries the status meaning success, declares its content as application/json, and its body is a json object whose only field, greeting, holds Hello, followed by a comma, a space and the name: GreetHandler(query: name=Ada) -> 200, content type application/json, {greeting: "Hello, Ada"}.

When the name is missing entirely, or is present but empty, the reply is a plain-text complaint instead: the status meaning the client's request was bad, a content type of text/plain; charset=utf-8, the header that tells a browser not to second-guess that declared type by inspecting the bytes, and a body holding the message "name is required" followed by a newline — and nothing further written after it: GreetHandler(query: name absent) -> 400, content type text/plain; charset=utf-8, "name is required". The standard library has a helper that produces exactly that reply — headers, status, message and trailing newline — from a message and a status.

Every part of each reply named above must actually reach the client. The reply writer is unforgiving about the sequence the three pieces are handed to it in, and it reports nothing when that sequence is wrong: the piece you set too late is simply dropped.
objective: Practice assembling a reply in the order the writer demands — headers, then status, then body — and branching to a plain-text error reply on bad input.
